title: A laboratory without weight
body: An accelerometer in a falling capsule can read zero even while the capsule accelerates towards Earth in ground-based coordinates. The equivalence principle turns this observation into a guide to gravity: freely falling laboratories provide the local setting for the laws of special relativity. The word local matters; it excludes comparing widely separated bodies over long times.

title: Universality and local physics
body: The weak equivalence principle states that ideal test bodies released at the same event with the same velocity fall alike, independently of composition. In Newtonian language their acceleration is \(\mathbf a=(m_g/m_i)\mathbf g\); universality makes the ratio common, and a choice of mass units sets \(m_g\overset{\text{mass convention}}{=}m_i\). This equality compares gravitational response with inertial resistance, not two separately derived formulas.

title: The Einstein principle
body: The Einstein equivalence principle adds that local nongravitational experiments in a freely falling, nonrotating laboratory obey special relativity, independently of its location and velocity. A supported laboratory feels weight because its floor prevents free fall. An accelerating laboratory in flat spacetime can reproduce that local experience without requiring spacetime curvature.

title: What a falling experiment tests
body: Release two small bodies beside an accelerometer inside a freely falling capsule. Neglect air drag, charge forces, spin effects and their own gravity. Locally they float together. Repeat the experiment with a larger separation and sensitive instruments: converging or diverging trajectories reveal \cref{tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity}. Equal free-fall response does not imply equal motion for bodies subject to different nongravitational forces.

title: What the principle does not prove
body: The equivalence principle motivates a metric description, but does not by itself derive Einstein's field equations. Nor can it remove curvature over a finite laboratory. Strong-equivalence statements involving self-gravitating bodies are stronger than the local nongravitational principle used here. See \cref{local inertial frames}{gr.local_inertial_frame} for its coordinate expression.

title: Coordinates adapted to free fall
body: An SR inertial frame covers flat spacetime. In a curved spacetime its replacement is a local inertial frame at a regular event. It makes the coordinate description match measurements by a freely falling observer there, while leaving neighbouring tidal effects intact.

title: The conditions at an event
body:
Choose coordinates centred on an event \(p\), with an orthonormal basis and the atlas signature \(+---\). Local inertial coordinates satisfy \[g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{local frame}}{=}\eta_{\mu
u},\qquad \partial_ho g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{normal coordinates}}{=}0.\] The labels identify coordinate choices, not field equations. Consequently the Levi-Civita connection coefficients vanish at that event.

title: A point is not a region
body: The metric near the event differs from its Minkowski value at quadratic order in the coordinate displacement. Curvature determines the leading departure; it cannot generally be removed along with the first derivatives. Approximating a laboratory by one inertial frame requires its size and duration to be small compared with the scales on which tidal effects become significant.

title: Free fall and hovering
body: A coasting astronaut can carry a nonrotating local frame whose accelerometer reads zero. A hovering astronaut must fire a rocket and has nonzero proper acceleration, even if their spatial coordinates stay fixed. Being momentarily at rest in some coordinates is therefore not the criterion for an inertial laboratory.

title: Orthonormal is not automatically inertial
body: Making the metric Minkowskian at one point fixes the basis there; eliminating first derivatives also constrains how coordinates extend nearby. An accelerated observer has an instantaneous orthonormal frame but not an inertial laboratory over time. \cref{Local flatness}{gr.local_flatness} states the geometric result; the \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle} connects it to physical experiments.

title: The observer's accelerometer
body: Free fall means that an ideal small body experiences no nongravitational force. It includes an orbiting spacecraft as well as a dropped object. The operational test is an accelerometer carried with the observer, not whether its position changes relative to the ground.

title: A timelike geodesic observer
body:
A freely falling observer follows a timelike worldline with tangent \(u^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d	au\). In the test-body approximation its covariant acceleration obeys \[a^\mu\coloneqq u^
u
abla_
u u^\mu\overset{	ext{free fall}}{=}0.\] Proper time \(	au\) is the observer's clock time. The first relation defines acceleration geometrically; the second imposes the force-free motion law.

title: Coordinate acceleration can remain
body: The connection contributes to covariant acceleration, so \(a^\mu=0\) does not generally imply \(d^2x^\mu/d\tau^2=0\). Ground-based coordinates describe a falling object as speeding up. That description and the object's zero accelerometer reading are compatible because they measure different notions of acceleration.

title: Weight on a surface
body: A person standing on a surface is held away from a free-fall trajectory by the ground's contact force. Their accelerometer reads a nonzero value. Conversely, an orbiting astronaut can feel weightless while the spacetime curvature produces measurable tidal acceleration between separated parts of the spacecraft.

title: Limits of the ideal observer
body: Treat the observer as small enough that spin, finite size, radiation reaction and self-gravity do not alter the test-particle motion. The geodesic model is an approximation for real extended bodies. Compare \cref{four-acceleration}{gr.four_acceleration} and \cref{tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity}: zero acceleration of one ideal observer does not mean zero relative acceleration of neighbouring observers.

title: Compare neighbouring falls
body: One object's coordinate acceleration can be changed by choosing a falling frame. Relative acceleration between nearby freely falling objects reveals something that survives that choice: spacetime curvature. Tides are therefore a local operational route from free fall to geometry.

title: Relative acceleration
body: In the Newtonian limit let \(\mathbf g\coloneqq-\boldsymbol\nabla\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is gravitational potential. Two nearby test bodies separated by \(\xi^j\) have \[\delta a^i\simeq-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\xi^j.\] The approximation retains first order in separation. A uniform acceleration removes the gradient of the potential at a point, but not this Hessian.

title: Stretching and squeezing
body: For a point mass, \(\Phi\coloneqq-GM/r\). A small radial separation has relative outward acceleration \(\delta a_r\simeq(2GM/r^3)\xi_r\): the inner body falls inward faster. A transverse separation is squeezed with coefficient \(-GM/r^3\). This comparison assumes separation much smaller than the radius and slow motion in a weak field.

title: Curvature is the relativistic refinement
body: In GR the \cref{geodesic deviation equation}{gr.geodesic_deviation} replaces the potential Hessian by components of the Riemann tensor measured in the observer's frame. It compares a family of freely falling trajectories, rather than assigning a gravitational force to one trajectory. Vacuum outside a body can have tides even though its matter density vanishes.

title: Relative velocity is not enough
body: Two inertial particles can separate at constant relative velocity in flat spacetime. That alone is not a tidal effect. The curvature measurement concerns relative acceleration after controlling initial conditions and accounting for the observer's frame. A picture of diverging paths must be read with that qualification.

title: Gravity changes the measuring structure
body: Special relativity studies matter on a fixed Minkowski geometry. General relativity makes geometry dynamical: the metric determines clock readings and causal directions, while its curvature and evolution respond to matter and boundary or initial data. Gravity concerns spacetime, not merely the shape of three-dimensional space.

title: Two linked laws
body: The geometric description has two parts. Ideal test bodies follow the metric's timelike or null geodesics. The metric itself obeys gravitational field equations. The \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle} motivates the first part and the local recovery of SR; it does not uniquely select the second.

title: From local freedom to finite-region effects
body: A falling frame removes the connection coefficients at an event. If all gravity were just acceleration of coordinates, that would finish the story. \cref{Tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity} shows otherwise: neighbouring free-fall trajectories respond differently, and this relative behaviour is encoded in curvature. Geometry distinguishes a coordinate effect from a measurable gravitational field.

title: A curved metric is not a rubber sheet
body: A rubber-sheet model suggests a mass pulling objects downward through an external gravitational field. GR needs no embedding space or additional downward force. Even clock-rate differences belong to the metric, and light follows null paths without possessing rest mass. Curved coordinate lines alone also prove nothing: flat spacetime can be written in curvilinear coordinates.

title: What the atlas separates
body: The \cref{spacetime metric}{gr.metric_tensor} explains measurement, connections explain comparison between neighbouring events, curvature describes the obstruction to flattening a region, and field equations supply dynamics. These are related but distinct questions. Matter is a source of curvature, but curvature can also persist and propagate in vacuum; the slogan must not imply that every curved region contains matter.

title: A field that measures intervals
body: The GR metric generalises the Minkowski metric to a smooth field on spacetime. At each event it pairs tangent vectors and determines clock intervals, spatial lengths in an observer's rest space, and light cones. Its coordinate components vary with position and with the chart.

title: A Lorentzian bilinear form
body:
The metric is a symmetric, nondegenerate covariant tensor \(g_{\mu
u}\) of signature \(+---\). For tangent vectors define \[g(V,W)\coloneqq g_{\mu
u}V^\mu W^
u.\] This contraction is coordinate-independent even though its components change. Nondegenerate means an inverse exists, not that every nonzero vector has nonzero norm: null vectors are essential.

title: Read the line element
body: With \(x^0\coloneqq ct\), the quadratic expression \(ds^2\coloneqq g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu\) has dimensions of length squared. In a chart with cross terms the coefficient of \(dt\,dr\) is twice the corresponding symmetric metric component when the coordinates themselves are \((t,r,\ldots)\). Always identify the coordinate convention before extracting components.

title: Varying components without curvature
body: Flat spacetime in spherical spatial coordinates has \(ds^2=c^2dt^2-dr^2-r^2d\theta^2-r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\). Its components depend on position, but the spacetime is flat. Conversely a curved spacetime can have Minkowski components at one event in a local inertial chart. Derivatives and their invariant combinations distinguish these cases.

title: Scope of this concept
body: The \cref{SR metric}{sr.metric_tensor} describes flat-spacetime measurement. Here the metric is a dynamical field; the \cref{inverse metric}{gr.inverse_metric}, \cref{line element}{gr.line_element} and curvature concepts develop its uses. In general the full metric cannot be made constant across a finite region by choosing better coordinates.

title: Returning from covectors to vectors
body: The metric converts a tangent vector into a covector. Its inverse reverses that conversion and allows contractions between covariant quantities. This is a matrix inverse in coordinates, not the reciprocal of every component.

title: The inverse relation
body:
Define \(g^{\mu
u}\) by \[g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha
u}\overset{	ext{inverse definition}}{=}\delta^\mu{}_{
u}.\] The Kronecker delta represents the identity map. The superscripts indicate a contravariant tensor; they are not decorative labels on the same numerical array.

title: Raise and lower indices
body:
For a covector \(w_
u\), define \(w^\mu\coloneqq g^{\mu
u}w_
u\). Lowering again gives \(g_{ho\mu}w^\mu\overset{	ext{inverse metric}}{=}w_ho\). The equality uses the inverse relation. Raising one index on a rank-two tensor similarly changes its type and often the signs of its components; preserve which index was raised.

title: A diagonal coordinate metric
body: For the \(t,r\) sector \(ds^2=f(r)c^2dt^2-f(r)^{-1}dr^2\), the inverse entries are \(g^{tt}=1/(fc^2)\) and \(g^{rr}=-f\) wherever that chart is nonsingular. A diagonal matrix permits reciprocals of diagonal entries. Cross terms require inversion of the whole matrix, and a coordinate singularity should not be mistaken for a physically degenerate spacetime metric.

title: Different objects at different points
body: Use the metric and inverse at the same event. A vector at one event and a covector at another cannot be contracted without a rule for comparing tangent spaces. That comparison belongs to \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport}; algebraic index movement is a separate operation.

title: Integrating physical volume
body: Coordinate boxes do not generally have physical volume equal to the product of their coordinate widths. The metric supplies the conversion factor. This makes an action or total integral independent of which coordinates label the region.

title: The invariant measure
body: Write \(g\coloneqq\det(g_{\mu\nu})\). In a nonsingular four-dimensional Lorentzian chart define \[dV_4\coloneqq\sqrt{|g|}\,d^4x=\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x.\] The last equality uses the negative determinant of a Lorentzian metric with one positive and three negative eigenvalues. This is the positive integration density; an oriented volume form additionally fixes orientation.

title: Why the Jacobian cancels
body: Under a coordinate change let \(J\coloneqq\det(\partial x'/\partial x)\). The tensor transformation law gives \(g'=g/J^2\), while coordinate volume changes by \(d^4x'=|J|d^4x\). Consequently \(\sqrt{|g'|}d^4x'\overset{\text{Jacobian cancellation}}{=}\sqrt{|g|}d^4x\). Neither factor alone is invariant.

title: Spherical coordinates in flat spacetime
body: Using coordinates \((ct,r,\theta,\phi)\), the flat metric has determinant \(-r^4\sin^2\theta\). Thus \(dV_4=r^2\sin\theta\,d(ct)\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi\) on the usual angular chart. The familiar spherical factor arises without curvature. If the time coordinate is \(t\), the metric determinant supplies the extra factor of \(c\).

title: Spacetime and spatial volume differ
body: A three-dimensional slice uses its induced spatial metric and a three-volume element, not simply the four-dimensional determinant with \(dt\) erased. The four-volume element belongs in covariant actions such as the \cref{Einstein-Hilbert action}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action}. A vanishing coordinate determinant at a polar axis may signal a failed chart rather than a failed geometry.

title: Turn a metric into a clock or ruler
body: The line element is the metric evaluated on an infinitesimal displacement. It packages the coordinate components into a quadratic expression that can be integrated along an appropriate curve. It is not generally a formula for finite coordinate differences between distant events.

title: The quadratic interval
body: Define \[ds^2\coloneqq g_{\mu\nu}(x)dx^\mu dx^\nu.\] With signature \(+---\), timelike displacements have positive squared interval, null displacements zero, and spacelike displacements negative. Along a timelike curve an ideal clock measures \(d\tau\coloneqq\sqrt{ds^2}/c\). For a spacelike curve its positive length element is \(d\ell\coloneqq\sqrt{-ds^2}\).

title: Pull back to a curve
body: For \(x^\mu(\lambda)\), insert \(dx^\mu=\dot x^\mu d\lambda\). The proper-time integral is \[\Delta\tau\coloneqq\frac1c\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}(x(\lambda))\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda.\] A monotonic change of parameter changes both the tangent and integration element, leaving the result unchanged. The path itself, however, matters.

title: Coordinate speed versus measured speed
body: For a radial null displacement in \(ds^2=fc^2dt^2-f^{-1}dr^2\), the null condition gives \(|dr/dt|\overset{\text{radial null}}{=}cf\). This coordinate speed need not equal \(c\). Outside the horizon a local static observer uses \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt f\) and \(d\tau=\sqrt f\,dt\), recovering \(|d\ell/d\tau|=c\).

title: Do not replace differentials by differences
body: If the metric varies along a path, substituting endpoint coordinate differences into a metric evaluated at one endpoint does not compute elapsed proper time. Integrate along the actual worldline. For large separations even the choice and existence of connecting geodesics can be nontrivial.

title: The time carried by a worldline
body: Proper time is an ideal clock's accumulated reading. It belongs to a timelike history, not to a coordinate grid. Observers can agree on two meeting events and still accumulate different proper times between them.

title: Clock time from the metric
body: For a future-directed timelike curve define \[\Delta\tau\coloneqq\frac1c\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu}.\] The expression uses the \(+---\) convention. It is independent of coordinates; a coordinate time \(t\) equals the clock reading only in appropriately chosen circumstances.

title: Motion in flat spacetime
body: In an inertial Cartesian chart, \(ds^2=c^2dt^2-d\mathbf x^2\). Therefore \[d\tau\overset{\text{Minkowski metric}}{=}dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}.\] The annotation identifies the chosen metric, not an approximation. For \(v\ll c\), expansion gives \(d\tau\simeq dt(1-v^2/(2c^2))\). This distinguishes an exact clock relation from its slow-motion limit.

title: A clock held at fixed position
body: For a static diagonal metric with time coordinate \(ct\), a stationary clock has \(d\tau\overset{\text{fixed position}}{=}\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt\). Different positions can have different rates relative to the same static time coordinate. Comparing those clocks requires a specified signal or meeting protocol; it is not a comparison of arbitrary coordinate labels.

title: Null paths carry no clock frame
body: The timelike clock integral approaches zero along null displacement, but a photon has no rest frame or ticking proper-time clock. Use an affine parameter for null geodesics. Timelike free-fall paths locally extremise proper time; they are not universally the globally longest paths between arbitrary events.

title: A nonzero direction with zero norm
body: A null curve has a nonzero tangent on the light cone at every point. Zero interval does not mean zero displacement. The Lorentzian signature allows cancellation between temporal and spatial contributions.

title: The null condition
body:
For a regular curve define \(k^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\lambda\). It is null when \[g_{\mu
u}k^\mu k^
u\overset{	ext{null condition}}{=}0,\qquad k^\mu
e0.\] Rescaling a monotonic parameter rescales the tangent but preserves its zero norm. This condition classifies the tangent; it does not specify how its direction evolves.

title: Light in a local frame
body: In a local inertial frame the condition is \(c^2dt^2-d\mathbf x^2=0\), hence lightlike motion has local speed \(c\). In general coordinates the corresponding coordinate speed may vary. At each event the metric, not a fixed drawing angle on the page, defines the light cone.

title: Null does not automatically mean geodesic
body: In geometric optics, freely propagating light in vacuum follows null geodesics. A prescribed null curve need not satisfy the geodesic equation. Bending or reflection by matter changes the physical situation, and finite-wavelength effects lie outside the ideal ray approximation. The geodesic law supplies information beyond the null constraint.

title: No photon proper-time parameter
body: A null path has vanishing proper-time increment, so proper time cannot parametrise it. An affine parameter gives a useful tangent and geodesic equation, with a constant rescaling freedom. See \cref{geodesics}{gr.geodesic} and \cref{causal structure}{gr.causal_structure} for dynamics and global influence respectively.

title: Which events can communicate?
body: The metric supplies local light cones. Their arrangement across spacetime determines which events can be connected by future-directed timelike or null curves. This global reachability is causal structure; no single coordinate separation reliably determines it in a general curved spacetime.

title: Local directions and global reachability
body: After choosing a consistent time orientation, a future-directed timelike curve can represent a massive observer and a future-directed causal curve may also include null segments. The chronological future of an event uses timelike curves; its causal future allows both timelike and null curves. These are existence statements about entire paths.

title: Build influence from local cones
body: At every point along a signal path the tangent must lie inside or on the future cone. A sequence of locally permitted directions may still fail to connect a chosen source to a distant receiver. Horizons arise from this global restriction, not from a local speed limit changing near the horizon.

title: Conformal rescaling
body: If \(\widetilde g_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\Omega^2g_{\mu\nu}\) with smooth \(\Omega>0\), tangent norms gain a positive factor. Their signs and null directions stay the same, so causal curves are preserved. Clock times and lengths generally change. Causal structure therefore contains less information than the full metric.

title: Cones do not guarantee good global causality
body: A Lorentzian metric alone does not rule out closed timelike curves or guarantee a global time function. Those are additional global properties. Likewise the coordinate tilt of a cone can change with the chart while physical reachability remains unchanged. Keep this distinction when studying an \cref{event horizon}{gr.event_horizon}.

title: Flat to first order
body: A smooth Lorentzian metric looks Minkowskian to first order in suitable coordinates around any regular event. This is a local approximation and an exact statement about values and first derivatives at a point, not a claim that curvature vanishes.

title: Normal-coordinate conditions
body:
At an event \(p\), choose \[g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{normal frame}}{=}\eta_{\mu
u},\qquad\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{normal coordinates}}{=}0.\] Nearby, \(g_{\mu
u}(x)=\eta_{\mu
u}+O(x^2)\). The equality at the point follows from the coordinate construction; the order symbol records corrections rather than silently setting them to zero.

title: Where curvature hides
body: The Riemann tensor contains second metric derivatives as well as products of first derivatives. In normal coordinates the latter vanish at the origin while the former need not. Thus a local inertial laboratory can recover SR at the event and still detect tides by comparing separated trajectories.

title: A scale for the approximation
body: If typical curvature components have magnitude of order \(1/L^2\), a laboratory of extent \(\ell\) has metric corrections of order \((\ell/L)^2\) in normal coordinates. This is a scale estimate, not a universal bound. Large boosts or rapidly varying curvature can change which components and duration matter for an actual experiment.

title: Pointwise flattening is not a field equation
body: Local flatness is available for any sufficiently smooth nondegenerate Lorentzian metric, regardless of whether it solves Einstein's equations. The physical equivalence principle additionally says that local nongravitational laws use this metric. Singular boundaries are outside the regular-point assumptions.

title: Fix signs before using formulas
body: Lorentzian geometry distinguishes one temporal direction from three spatial directions. Either overall sign convention describes the same causal physics when every dependent definition is translated consistently. This atlas uses \(+---\) in both SR and GR.

title: The atlas convention
body: In an orthonormal frame set \[\eta_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).\] For a nonzero vector, positive norm is timelike, zero norm null and negative norm spacelike. The signature counts positive and negative directions of the quadratic form; it is not the signs of arbitrary diagonal entries in a chart with cross terms.

title: Time and units
body: Use \(x^0\coloneqq ct\) when retaining SI dimensions, and announce \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\) when switching to natural units. Then a proper-time tangent obeys \(g_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\overset{\text{proper-time normalisation}}{=}c^2\), or one in natural units. The numerical convention does not change the physical speed of light.

title: Translate a source carefully
body: Tong uses \(-+++\), whereas these concepts use \(+---\). Multiplying the metric by minus one changes scalar contractions and stress-energy formulas expressed with the metric. A perfect fluid consequently has a minus pressure term in the atlas convention. Connection coefficients are unchanged by a constant overall metric sign flip.

title: Signature does not fix curvature sign
body: Authors also choose an independent sign and index convention for the Riemann tensor. That choice propagates to Ricci curvature, the Einstein equations and the action. Check the full convention bundle in the notation glossary, not just the signature, before importing a formula. No physical conclusion should depend on mixing conventions from two sources.

title: Compare fields at neighbouring events
body: Vectors at different points belong to different tangent spaces. A chart gives component labels, but subtraction of those components alone depends on how the chart varies. A connection supplies the additional comparison rule needed for differentiation and transport.

title: A derivative with a direction
body:
Write \(
abla_XV\) for the covariant derivative of a vector field \(V\) in direction \(X\). It is linear in the direction and obeys the product rule \[
abla_X(fV)=X(f)V+f
abla_XV.\] The term \(X(f)\) differentiates the scalar coefficient, while the other term differentiates the vector field itself. These properties let a local rule extend consistently to tensor fields.

title: Connection coefficients
body:
In a coordinate basis define \(
abla_{\partial_\mu}\partial_
u\coloneqq\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\partial_ho\). The coefficients describe the change of the basis under the chosen comparison rule. They are not tensor components: coordinate changes add a term involving second coordinate derivatives.

title: The standard GR choice
body: A connection can exist without a metric. Standard GR uses the unique torsion-free connection compatible with the metric, called the Levi-Civita connection. Thus the metric supplies both measurements and the comparison rule. Metric compatibility alone would not select a unique connection if torsion were allowed.

title: Connection is not curvature
body: Nonzero coefficients can occur in flat spacetime, for example in polar coordinates. Curvature concerns the failure of transport to agree around infinitesimal loops and is tensorial. A local inertial chart can remove coefficients at an event without removing curvature. See \cref{Christoffel symbols}{gr.christoffel_symbols} for computation and \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport} for the pathwise interpretation.

title: Compute the metric's connection
body: Christoffel symbols turn a metric into a practical differentiation and free-fall rule. Their numerical values depend on the coordinate basis; the geometric connection they represent does not depend on a particular chart.

title: The Levi-Civita formula
body:
Metric compatibility and zero torsion give \[\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{Levi-Civita}}{=} rac12g^{ho\sigma}(\partial_\mu g_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u g_{\sigma\mu}-\partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}).\] This equality follows from those two conditions, rather than defining every possible connection. The inverse metric contracts the free index of the metric-derivative combination.

title: Where the formula comes from
body: Expand \(\nabla_\mu g_{\nu\sigma}=0\) and its two cyclic permutations. Add the first two equations and subtract the third. Symmetry of the lower connection indices cancels the unwanted terms. Multiplication by \(g^{\rho\sigma}/2\) isolates the coefficient above. Both compatibility and torsion-freedom are needed for this step.

title: Flat space in polar coordinates
body: For the spatial plane with metric \(d\ell^2=dr^2+r^2d\phi^2\), the nonzero coefficients include \(\Gamma^r{}_{\phi\phi}=-r\) and \(\Gamma^\phi{}_{r\phi}=1/r\). They account for changing radial and angular basis vectors even though the plane is flat. The same coefficients occur for the corresponding negative spatial sector of a flat Lorentzian metric.

title: Do not test curvature by inspection
body: A coefficient that vanishes in one chart can be nonzero in another. A genuine tensor that vanishes at an event vanishes there in every nonsingular chart. Build the Riemann tensor before concluding that gravity is intrinsic. For calculations, first invert the metric, then take derivatives, and use lower-index symmetry to reduce repeated work.

title: Differentiate the field, not just its components
body: Ordinary component derivatives acquire unwanted terms when a coordinate basis changes. Covariant differentiation adds connection terms so that the result is a tensor and can enter a coordinate-independent physical law.

title: Vectors and covectors
body:
For a vector and a covector define \[

title: Why the covector sign differs
body:
The contraction \(w_

title: A scalar's second derivative
body:
A scalar satisfies \(

abla_\mu

u f=\partial_\mu\partial_
u f-\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu

title: Covariant is not constant
body:
A field with constant coordinate components need not have zero covariant derivative. Conversely a parallel field may have changing components. Along a curve with tangent \(u\), the directional derivative is \(D V^\mu/D\lambda\coloneqq u^
u
abla_
u V^\mu\). This is the derivative in \cref{parallel transport}{gr.parallel_transport}.

title: Transport preserves measurement
body: A metric measures inner products at each point. Compatibility asks that the connection's transport respect those measurements, so a vector carried parallel along a path does not change its norm merely because it reaches another tangent space.

title: The compatibility condition
body:
A metric-compatible connection satisfies \[
abla_ho g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{compatibility}}{=}0.\] In components this is \(\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}=\Gamma^\sigma{}_{ho\mu}g_{\sigma
u}+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{ho
u}g_{\mu\sigma}\). Ordinary metric derivatives need not vanish; connection terms balance them.

title: Preservation along a curve
body:
For parallel vectors \(V,W\) and curve tangent \(u\), the product rule gives \[ rac{d}{d\lambda}g(V,W)=(
abla_u g)(V,W)+g(

abla_uW)\overset{	ext{compatible transport}}{=}0.\] Compatibility removes the first term and parallel transport removes the others. Both hypotheses matter.

title: Index movement commutes with differentiation
body: Since \(\nabla g=0\), lowering an index before or after covariant differentiation gives the same result. Differentiating the inverse relation also gives \(\nabla g^{-1}=0\). These identities simplify stress-energy conservation and four-velocity normalisation throughout GR.

title: Norm preservation does not imply no curvature
body: A vector may return rotated after transport around a loop while keeping its norm. Compatibility preserves metric comparisons, not path independence. Compatibility also does not force torsion to vanish; imposing both conditions selects the \cref{Levi-Civita connection}{gr.christoffel_symbols}.

title: A second condition on transport
body: Standard GR uses both metric compatibility and zero torsion. These are independent conditions. Torsion describes an antisymmetric part of the comparison rule; curvature describes how transport around a loop changes a vector.

title: A tensor built from the connection
body:
To avoid confusing torsion with stress-energy, write \[\mathcal T(X,Y)\coloneqq
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y].\] In a coordinate basis, where the basis commutators vanish, \(\mathcal T^ho{}_{\mu
u}=\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}-\Gamma^ho{}_{
u\mu}\). Zero torsion therefore makes the lower coefficient indices symmetric in that basis.

title: Why the basis qualification matters
body: In a noncoordinate frame the basis vectors need not commute. Their commutator contributes to the torsion formula, so simply antisymmetrising coefficients is insufficient. Torsion itself is a tensor even though the coefficients used to calculate it are not.

title: A scalar commutator
body:
For a scalar \(f\), the difference of its second covariant derivatives is \((
abla_\mu
abla_
u-
abla_
u
abla_\mu)f=-\mathcal T^ho{}_{\mu
u}\partial_ho f\) in a coordinate basis. It vanishes for the standard torsion-free connection. Vectors can still have a nonzero derivative commutator because curvature acts on their indices.

title: Zero torsion does not mean flat spacetime
body: Schwarzschild spacetime uses a torsion-free connection and has nonzero curvature. The two conditions measure different failures of Euclidean intuition. The schematic infinitesimal parallelogram picture refers to the leading closure defect, not a guarantee that every finite loop behaves as in flat space.

title: Carry a vector along a specified path
body: Parallel transport uses a connection to compare vectors in successive tangent spaces. Once the path and initial vector are specified, it determines the transported vector through an ordinary differential equation.

title: The transport equation
body: For a curve \(x^\mu(\lambda)\) and vector \(V^\mu(\lambda)\), parallel transport means \[\frac{DV^\mu}{D\lambda}\coloneqq\frac{dV^\mu}{d\lambda}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda}V^\beta\overset{\text{parallel}}{=}0.\] The connection correction distinguishes constant geometric direction from constant coordinate components.

title: Moving round a sphere
body: On a sphere, carry a tangent arrow along a geodesic triangle. It can return to its starting point with a different orientation. Each segment was parallel transport; the discrepancy reflects curvature integrated over the loop. This positive-definite example illustrates the comparison rule, while spacetime uses a Lorentzian metric and can mix temporal and spatial directions.

title: Preserved norm, path-dependent result
body: The Levi-Civita connection preserves inner products of parallel vectors, so timelike, spacelike and null character are preserved. Different routes between the same endpoints can nevertheless yield different final vectors. Curvature controls this effect for infinitesimal loops; topology can also matter for transport around noncontractible loops.

title: Transport is not the motion law for every object
body: A vector carried by a rotating or accelerating instrument need not be parallel transported. A geodesic is the special case where the curve's own tangent is parallel along itself. Specify both the transported object and the path before interpreting a change in components or a loop comparison.

title: Straightest motion in curved spacetime
body: A geodesic is defined by its tangent's transport, not by how straight a curve looks on a coordinate plot. With the Levi-Civita connection, timelike geodesics describe ideal freely falling massive bodies and null geodesics describe vacuum light rays in geometric optics.

title: An affine tangent
body: For \(v^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\lambda\), the affine geodesic condition is \[\nabla_vv\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0.\] The parameter \(\lambda\) is affine; another parameter of the form \(a\lambda+b\), with constant nonzero \(a\), is affine too. A general reparameterisation leaves the curve but adds a tangent-proportional term to its equation.

title: Choose the causal type initially
body: Metric compatibility gives \(d[g(v,v)]/d\lambda\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0\). Thus the initial tangent determines whether the path remains timelike, null or spacelike. Proper time is an affine parameter for a timelike geodesic. Null curves have no nonzero proper-time increment and need a different affine parameter.

title: Local straightness and global shape
body: In local inertial coordinates, an affine geodesic has zero coordinate acceleration at the chosen event. Elsewhere its plotted path may bend because the connection coefficients change. In a sufficiently small normal neighbourhood the initial position and tangent determine a unique geodesic, but global connecting geodesics can be multiple or absent.

title: Stationary is not globally shortest
body: For timelike paths the variational statement concerns stationary proper time, locally maximal for short enough segments without conjugate points. It is not a universal shortest-distance rule. Spacelike geodesics are useful geometric curves, not possible histories of massive observers.

title: A differential equation for free paths
body: The coordinate form of geodesic motion balances ordinary coordinate acceleration against connection terms. Given a smooth metric, initial event and tangent, it is a second-order system for the path.

title: Affine parameter form
body: Expanding \(\nabla_vv=0\) yields \[\frac{d^2x^\mu}{d\lambda^2}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}\frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda}\frac{dx^\beta}{d\lambda}\overset{\text{affine geodesic}}{=}0.\] The annotation states the motion law and parameter assumption. The Christoffel contribution is not a nongravitational force measured by an accelerometer.

title: A straight line in polar coordinates
body: In a flat spatial plane the radial and angular equations are \(\ddot r-r\dot\phi^2=0\) and \(\ddot\phi+2\dot r\dot\phi/r=0\). Dots denote an affine parameter. These apparently accelerated coordinate motions describe Cartesian straight lines. They provide a useful check before interpreting a nonzero connection term as curvature.

title: Check normalisation and parameter
body: For a timelike path with proper time, impose \(g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu=c^2\); for a null affine tangent impose zero norm. These constraints are preserved by exact geodesic evolution and are useful checks on a calculation. With arbitrary parameter \(s\), the right-hand side becomes \(f(s)dx^\mu/ds\), which changes the parameter rather than the unparameterised path.

title: Coordinate time is usually not affine
body: Replacing proper time by a convenient coordinate time without the extra term changes the equation. Also keep the test-body assumptions: contact forces, thrust and finite-size effects require additional dynamics. See \cref{four-acceleration}{gr.four_acceleration} for the covariant force measure.

title: Free fall from stationary clock time
body: The massive-particle action weights the proper length of a timelike path. Holding the metric and endpoint events fixed, varying the intervening path gives the geodesic equation. This connects geometric free fall to the earlier action principle.

title: The invariant path action
body: For a massive test particle define \[S[x]\coloneqq-mc\int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,d\lambda=-mc^2\int d\tau.\] The equality uses the definition of proper time. The square root makes the functional invariant under monotonic reparameterisation; the stationary condition is \(\delta S\overset{\text{fixed endpoints}}{=}0\).

title: A convenient quadratic calculation
body:
For an affine parameter one may obtain the same geodesic equation by varying \(L\coloneqq	frac12 g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u\). Then \(\partial L/\partial\dot x^ho=g_{ho
u}\dot x^
u\) and \(\partial L/\partial x^ho=	frac12\partial_ho g_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u\). The Euler-Lagrange equation, multiplied by the inverse metric, gives \(\ddot x^\sigma+\Gamma^\sigma{}_{\mu
u}\dot x^\mu\dot x^
u=0\). The symmetric velocity product produces the Levi-Civita combination.

title: Do not vary a zero null length
body: The massive square-root action cannot simply be restricted to null curves before variation: it then supplies no useful path functional. The quadratic action with an initially null tangent yields affine null geodesics, or an auxiliary-variable action can enforce the null constraint. Distinguish this from assigning a proper-time clock to light.

title: What is varied
body: The path, not the spacetime metric, is varied here. Metric variation belongs to the Einstein-Hilbert action. Stationary proper time also does not promise a global maximum for long paths; local extrema and conjugate points matter.

title: A local tangent normalised by a clock
body: Four-velocity describes a massive observer's motion as a vector in the tangent space at each event. Its normalisation follows from proper time, so it is more constrained than the tangent formed with an arbitrary curve parameter.

title: Definition and normalisation
body: Define \(u^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\tau\). With signature \(+---\), \[g_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu\overset{\text{proper time}}{=}c^2.\] Natural units set the right-hand side to one. The constant norm does not require constant components; the observer may accelerate or move through a varying metric.

title: An instantaneous local measurement
body: In an orthonormal frame, \(u^{\hat a}=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) with \(\gamma\coloneqq(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\). Hatted indices denote frame components. This familiar SR expression applies locally; replacing frame components by arbitrary coordinate components can give incorrect measured speeds.

title: Compare observers at one event
body: Two future-directed unit clock tangents \(u,w\) meeting at an event have relative Lorentz factor \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}\coloneqq g(u,w)/c^2\). It equals one for comoving observers and exceeds one for relative motion. Comparing velocities at separated events additionally requires a transport or observation prescription.

title: No massive four-velocity for light
body: A photon has a null tangent or four-momentum, not a four-velocity parametrised by proper time. The distinction prevents dividing by a vanishing proper-time increment. The GR concept keeps the local SR interpretation while making tangent-space location explicit.

title: Acceleration that an instrument measures
body: Four-acceleration measures how a massive observer departs from geodesic motion. Unlike a second coordinate derivative, it is a vector. Its magnitude is the proper acceleration registered by an ideal accelerometer.

title: Covariant change of velocity
body: Define \[a^\mu\coloneqq\frac{Du^\mu}{D\tau}=\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\alpha\beta}u^\alpha u^\beta.\] Free fall imposes \(a^\mu\overset{\text{geodesic}}{=}0\). In the atlas convention define the measured magnitude by \(\alpha\coloneqq\sqrt{-g_{\mu\nu}a^\mu a^\nu}\).

title: Orthogonality to velocity
body: Differentiate the normalisation \(g(u,u)=c^2\). Metric compatibility and the product rule give \[0\overset{\text{fixed norm}}{=}\frac{d}{d\tau}g(u,u)=2g(u,a).\] Thus acceleration is orthogonal to the timelike velocity and is spacelike unless zero. In the instantaneous rest frame its time component vanishes.

title: A supported observer
body: A rocket held at constant radius outside a spherical body has nonzero proper acceleration, although its radial coordinate is fixed. An orbiting test body can have zero proper acceleration despite a changing coordinate velocity. The distinction is between support or thrust and geometrically free motion, not between moving and stationary pictures.

title: Notation and scope
body: Use lowercase \(a^\mu\) here, reserving electromagnetic \(A^\mu\) for the potential. The magnitude is coordinate-independent, but its spatial direction is measured relative to a frame. Accelerating frames and finite-body tidal stresses need separate treatment; zero four-acceleration does not imply zero curvature.

title: Measure curvature with a family of falls
body: Geodesic deviation compares nearby free-fall paths rather than one observer's coordinate acceleration. It makes tidal gravity quantitative. Work to first order in separation, with a smooth family of affinely parametrised geodesics.

title: The separation equation
body: Let \(u\) be the geodesic tangent and \(\xi\) the connecting vector of a family whose parameter directions commute. With the glossary's Riemann convention, \[\frac{D^2\xi^\rho}{D\tau^2}\overset{\text{geodesic deviation}}{=}R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}u^\sigma u^\mu\xi^\nu.\] A source with the opposite Riemann definition writes the opposite sign. The index order is part of the convention.

title: Why curvature enters
body:
Zero torsion and \([u,\xi]=0\) give \(
abla_u\xi=
abla_\xi u\). Differentiate once more along \(u\), commute the derivatives, and use \(
abla_u u=0\). The remaining commutator is \(R(u,\xi)u\), giving the displayed equation. Its ingredients are the geodesic law, torsion-free comparison, and curvature, not an additional force law.

title: Recover Newtonian tides
body: For slowly moving neighbours in a weak static field, the spatial equation becomes \(d^2\xi^i/dt^2\simeq-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\xi^j\). A point mass stretches radial separations and squeezes transverse ones. This limit checks the convention's physical sign against the earlier tidal-gravity example.

title: Relative motion needs initial data
body: Even in flat spacetime neighbouring geodesics can have nonzero initial relative velocity; their separation then changes linearly. Curvature determines covariant relative acceleration. For finite separations the linear deviation approximation fails, and non-geodesic observers introduce additional acceleration terms.

title: Curvature survives a change of coordinates
body: A connection compares vectors at neighbouring events. Curvature measures the local failure of those comparisons to agree around a loop. It controls tidal acceleration even in a freely falling frame where the connection coefficients vanish at one event.

title: Fix the derivative order
body:
For the Levi-Civita connection our convention is \[[
abla_\mu,
abla_
u]V^ho\coloneqq(
abla_\mu
abla_
u-
abla_
u
abla_\mu)V^ho=R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}V^\sigma.\] Some books define the opposite sign. Here the order of the last two indices follows the derivative order shown; reversing those indices reverses the sign.

title: From connection to tensor
What the indices measure
body: The indices \(\mu,\nu\) select the oriented plane of a small loop, \(\sigma\) the transported vector component and \(\rho\) the resulting change. With its first index lowered, Riemann is antisymmetric within each index pair, symmetric under exchange of pairs, and obeys a cyclic identity. These symmetries leave 20 independent components in four dimensions.

title: Zero coefficients are not zero curvature
body: In normal coordinates \(\Gamma(p)=0\), but its derivatives at \(p\) generally remain. Flatness requires Riemann to vanish throughout a neighbourhood, not merely a convenient choice of coefficients. The same tensor supplies the relative acceleration in \cref{geodesic deviation}{gr.geodesic_deviation}; contractions give the \cref{Ricci tensor}{gr.ricci_tensor}.

title: Trace the tidal map
body: Riemann describes directional tidal stretching and transport. Ricci is a contraction that retains the trace of this information. It is especially useful for the volume behaviour of nearby freely falling trajectories and for coupling geometry to matter.

title: Contract a specific pair
body: With the atlas curvature convention, define \[R_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq R^\rho{}_{\mu\rho\nu}.\] The summed index is the first upper and third lower slot of Riemann as written. For the Levi-Civita connection the result is symmetric, so it has ten independent components in four dimensions.

title: Volume change versus shape change
body:
An initially comoving small cloud can stretch in one direction while shrinking in another. The trace of its tidal acceleration involves \(R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\), while directional distortions require more of Riemann. For an initially nonexpanding, shear-free, rotation-free timelike geodesic bundle, the initial expansion rate obeys \(d	heta/d	au=-R_{\mu
u}u^\mu u^
u\). In general shear, rotation and existing expansion also contribute.

title: Vacuum can still produce tides
body: Outside an isolated spherical mass, with zero cosmological constant, \(R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0\). Nevertheless a falling cloud stretches radially and contracts transversely. The remaining trace-free part of Riemann, called Weyl curvature, carries this tidal information. Ricci-flat therefore does not mean flat.

title: The next contraction
body: Contracting Ricci with the inverse metric gives the \cref{Ricci scalar}{gr.ricci_scalar}. Combining that scalar with Ricci gives the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor}. Each contraction discards information; none is an interchangeable name for the full curvature tensor.

title: A scalar from curvature
body: The Ricci scalar assigns a coordinate-independent number to each event by tracing the Ricci tensor with the metric. It is compact enough to serve as a gravitational action integrand, but contains much less information than either Ricci or Riemann.

title: A metric trace
body: Define \[R\coloneqq g^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}.\] This is a tensor contraction, not the ordinary sum of diagonal entries in an arbitrary chart. In a local orthonormal frame of signature \(+---\), it reads \(R\overset{\text{orthonormal frame}}{=}R_{\hat0\hat0}-R_{\hat1\hat1}-R_{\hat2\hat2}-R_{\hat3\hat3}\). The hats denote frame components rather than coordinate labels.

title: Curvature proportional to the metric
body:
If a four-dimensional geometry has \(R_{\mu
u}=A g_{\mu
u}\), where \(A\) is a scalar, then \[R\overset{	ext{given Ricci}}{=}A g^{\mu
u}g_{\mu
u}=4A.\] The factor four counts dimensions; signature does not change the trace of the identity. In \(n\) dimensions this example gives \(nA\).

title: Cancellation loses information
body: A vanishing trace can hide nonzero Ricci components, and even zero Ricci can hide Weyl curvature. Thus \(R=0\) alone establishes neither vacuum nor flatness. Its sign also depends on the chosen curvature and metric conventions; it is not a convention-free label for attractive or repulsive gravity.

title: From scalar to action
body: The product \(R\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x\) is an invariant integration density. Its integral enters the \cref{Einstein-Hilbert action}{gr.einstein_hilbert_action}, whose variation contains the full Ricci tensor rather than only the scalar. With length-valued coordinates, \(R\) has dimensions of inverse length squared.

title: A divergence-free curvature combination
body: Ricci alone generally has a nonzero covariant divergence. Subtracting half its metric trace produces the Einstein tensor, whose divergence vanishes identically. This makes it compatible with a locally conserved stress-energy source.

title: Subtract the trace term
body:
Define \[G_{\mu
u}\coloneqq R_{\mu
u}-	frac12 Rg_{\mu
u}.\] It is symmetric for the Levi-Civita connection and depends on the metric and its derivatives through second order. The symbol \(G_{\mu
u}\) denotes a tensor; the unindexed constant \(G\) denotes Newton's gravitational constant.

title: Why one half appears
body:
The contracted \cref{Bianchi identity}{gr.bianchi_identity} gives \(
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}=	frac12
abla_
u R\). Metric compatibility then yields \[
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\overset{
abla g=0}{=}
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-	frac12
abla_
u R\overset{	ext{Bianchi}}{=}0.\] This holds for every smooth metric with its Levi-Civita connection, before imposing any field equation.

title: The trace in four dimensions
body: Tracing the definition gives \[G^\mu{}_{\mu}=R-\tfrac12(4)R=-R.\] Consequently \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\) implies \(R=0\) and then \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\) in four dimensions. This argument changes with dimension; in two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.

title: An identity does not determine gravity
body:
The divergence identity neither sets \(G_{\mu
u}\) to zero nor identifies it with matter. That additional physical relation is the \cref{Einstein field equation}{gr.einstein_field_equations}. A constant multiple of the metric also has zero divergence, allowing a cosmological term. Divergence-free is weaker than covariantly constant: \(
abla_ho G_{\mu
u}\) need not vanish.

title: Curvature has internal consistency
body: Curvature is built from a connection rather than specified independently at each event. Its derivatives therefore satisfy identities. The differential Bianchi identity is the one that makes the Einstein tensor's divergence vanish.

title: A cyclic differential identity
body:
For the Levi-Civita connection, \[
abla_\lambda R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}+
abla_\mu R^ho{}_{\sigma
u\lambda}+
abla_
u R^ho{}_{\sigma\lambda\mu}\equiv0.\] The cyclic sum runs over the derivative index and the last two curvature indices. This is distinct from the algebraic, or first, Bianchi identity, which cycles three slots of Riemann without taking derivatives.

title: Why an identity exists
body: Covariant derivative commutators obey the Jacobi identity: the cyclic sum of nested commutators vanishes. Inserting their curvature action gives the differential identity above. Equivalently, in normal coordinates the relevant second derivatives of the connection cancel cyclically. Neither route uses matter properties or Einstein's equations.

title: Contract to a useful form
body:
Contracting with the metric and using Riemann's symmetries produces \[2
abla^\mu R_{\mu
u}-
abla_
u R\equiv0.\] By the definition of the \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and metric compatibility this becomes \(
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}\equiv0\). The contraction hides much of the original index structure while retaining the identity needed for source consistency.

title: Geometry and matter play different roles
body:
For constant \(\Lambda\), both \(G_{\mu
u}\) and \(\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\) are divergence-free. Applying the field equation then requires \(
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}=0\). This is a compatibility statement about a coupled solution; the geometric identity alone is not a matter equation of motion or a guarantee of a globally conserved total energy.

title: Test geometry rather than chart components
body: A component can diverge because coordinates fail. Scalar contractions of curvature take the same value at an event in every regular chart, so their divergence is stronger evidence of a geometric problem.

title: Useful contractions
body:
Common examples are the Ricci scalar \(R\), the squared Ricci contraction \(R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u}\), and the Kretschmann scalar \[K\coloneqq R_{\mu
uho\sigma}R^{\mu
uho\sigma}.\] All indices are contracted with the metric. Despite the language of a square, such Lorentzian contractions need not be positive for arbitrary tensors or geometries.

title: Schwarzschild separates two suspect radii
body: For Schwarzschild with \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), direct curvature evaluation gives \[R\overset{\text{vacuum}}{=}0,\qquad K\overset{\text{Schwarzschild}}{=}\frac{48m^2}{r^6}.\] Thus the apparent metric divergence at \(r=2m\) has finite \(K=3/(4m^4)\), whereas \(K\) diverges as \(r\to0\). The first is a chart failure that a regular extension removes; the second is divergent tidal curvature.

title: Check dimensions and scale
body: Since curvature has dimensions of inverse length squared, \(K\) has dimensions of inverse length to the fourth power. Doubling \(r\) at fixed mass reduces Schwarzschild's \(K\) by 64. This quantifies local curvature, not the strength of a coordinate acceleration or the existence of a horizon.

title: A diagnostic is not a complete regularity theorem
body: Finite scalar invariants do not prove extendibility or geodesic completeness, and some curved Lorentzian geometries have vanishing polynomial curvature invariants. A complete singularity analysis examines causal geodesics and possible extensions. See \cref{coordinate singularity}{gr.coordinate_singularity} and \cref{black-hole singularity}{gr.black_hole_singularity} for the Schwarzschild distinction.

title: Let the metric be dynamical
body: A particle action varies a path in a given metric. The Einstein-Hilbert action instead varies the metric itself, providing field equations for spacetime geometry. Matter contributes its own action to the same stationary-variation problem.

title: Keep action and curvature signs together
body: Use \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G\), signature \(+---\), and the atlas Riemann convention. Define \[S_g\coloneqq-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(R+2\Lambda).\] This pairs with \(\delta S_m=\tfrac12\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}\). Other consistent conventions use different signs; copying the action alone from them changes the theory's relative coupling.

title: Two variations make the Einstein tensor
body:
Varying the inverse metric gives \(\delta\sqrt{-g}=-	frac12\sqrt{-g}\,g_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}\) and \(\delta R=R_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}+g^{\mu
u}\delta R_{\mu
u}\). The last term is a divergence. Hence, for variations of compact support, \[\delta S_g\overset{	ext{boundary vanishes}}{=}- rac{1}{2\kappa}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u})\delta g^{\mu
u}.\] The determinant variation supplies the trace term that Ricci alone lacks.

title: Stationarity supplies the field equation
body:
Adding the matter variation and requiring \(\delta(S_g+S_m)\overset{	ext{stationary}}{=}0\) for arbitrary interior metric variations yields \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The gravitational action selects dynamics; the Bianchi identity checks their consistency. See \cref{stress-energy variation}{gr.stress_energy_variation} for the source definition.

title: Boundary conditions are part of the problem
body: Compactly supported variations justify the local derivation above. On a region with a boundary, fixing only the induced metric does not generally remove the normal derivatives of its variation from the bare action. A suitable gravitational boundary term is then required. The cosmological term is optional physics, while the boundary treatment is necessary for the stated variational problem.

title: The local source of curvature
body: Stress-energy packages the energy and momentum carried by matter and non-gravitational fields. GR places this tensor on curved spacetime and couples it to geometry. The \cref{SR energy-momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} develops its flat-spacetime role; the two concepts remain separate but linked.

title: What an observer measures
body: For an observer with four-velocity \(v\), normalised by \(g(v,v)=c^2\), define the measured energy density \[\epsilon_{(v)}\coloneqq\frac{1}{c^2}T_{\mu\nu}v^\mu v^\nu.\] This contraction is a scalar once the observer is specified. Different observers can measure different densities at the same event without disagreeing about the tensor.

title: Components in a local rest frame
body: In an orthonormal frame with \(x^{\hat0}=ct\), \(T^{\hat0\hat0}\) is energy density, \(cT^{\hat0\hat i}\) is energy flux and \(T^{\hat i\hat j}\) is momentum flux or stress. Symmetry relates energy flux to momentum density. These interpretations apply to orthonormal components; arbitrary coordinate components need the appropriate frame factors.

title: More than rest mass gravitates
body: Pressure, radiation and field energy all contribute to \(T_{\mu\nu}\). A \cref{perfect fluid}{gr.perfect_fluid} provides a simple model, while \cref{metric variation of matter}{gr.stress_energy_variation} supplies a general construction. The source includes all interacting matter sectors together; one sector may exchange energy with another.

title: Do not add a local gravity tensor by analogy
body: The right-hand source in Einstein's equation is not a general local tensor density of gravitational energy. Gravitational dynamics also reside in the metric's nonlinear field equation. Accordingly \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation} does not by itself provide a conserved total energy for every spacetime.

title: Isotropy defines the idealisation
body: A perfect fluid has a local rest frame with energy density \(\epsilon\), isotropic pressure \(p\), and no heat flux or viscous stress. Its continuum description is useful when a small fluid element contains many particles yet is small compared with macroscopic gradients.

title: Build the covariant tensor
body:
With signature \(+---\) and \(g(u,u)=c^2\), the model is \[T^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{perfect fluid}}{=} rac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}u^\mu u^
u-pg^{\mu
u}.\] In the local fluid rest frame, \(u^{\hat\mu}=(c,0,0,0)\), so \(T^{\hat\mu\hat
u}=\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon,p,p,p)\). The minus metric term gives positive spatial pressures in this signature.

title: Dust and radiation
body: Dust neglects pressure and gives \(T^{\mu\nu}=\epsilon u^\mu u^\nu/c^2\), with \(\epsilon\simeq\rho c^2\) when rest mass dominates. Isotropic radiation instead has \(p=\epsilon/3\). Both fit the same tensor form, but their matter response differs through their \cref{equation of state}{gr.equation_of_state}.

title: Project conservation along the flow
body:
Contract \(
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=0\) with \(u_
u\). Metric compatibility and fixed velocity norm remove the acceleration contraction, leaving \[u^\mu
abla_\mu\epsilon+(\epsilon+p)
abla_\mu u^\mu\overset{	ext{energy balance}}{=}0.\] The first term follows a fluid element's density; the second accounts for expansion and pressure work. Projecting perpendicular to \(u\) gives the fluid acceleration caused by pressure gradients.

title: Perfect does not mean pressureless or geodesic
body: The absence of viscosity is not the absence of pressure. Pressure gradients can accelerate the fluid, so its elements need not follow geodesics. Freely moving dust does follow geodesics wherever its density is nonzero, until effects such as stream crossing invalidate a single-fluid velocity description.

title: State the matter assumptions of a theorem
body: Energy conditions impose inequalities on stress-energy. They make assumptions such as nonnegative observer energy or causal energy flow precise. They are additional hypotheses, not identities or consequences of Einstein's equations.

title: Null and weak conditions
body:
The null energy condition (NEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}k^\mu k^
u\geq0\) for every null \(k\). The weak energy condition (WEC) requires \(T_{\mu
u}v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) for every timelike \(v\). Normalising \(v\) turns the latter into nonnegative measured energy density. By continuity WEC implies NEC.

title: Dominant and strong conditions
body:
With \(+---\), the dominant energy condition (DEC) requires \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^\mu{}_{
u}v^
u\) to be future-directed causal or zero for every future timelike \(v\). The strong energy condition (SEC) requires \((T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u})v^\mu v^
u\geq0\) in four dimensions. Through the field equations with zero cosmological constant, SEC gives the Ricci convergence condition used in focusing arguments. With \(\Lambda
e0\), include its effective source before drawing that conclusion.

title: Perfect-fluid tests
body: For a perfect fluid the conditions reduce to: NEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\); WEC, also \(\epsilon\geq0\); DEC, \(\epsilon\geq|p|\); SEC, \(\epsilon+p\geq0\) and \(\epsilon+3p\geq0\). These follow by testing rest-frame and highly boosted observers. Positive vacuum energy has \(p=-\epsilon\), so it satisfies NEC, WEC and DEC but violates SEC.

title: Names do not form a strength ranking
body: The strong condition is not stronger than the weak condition in the logical sense. Classical models can violate some conditions, and quantum expectation values can violate pointwise conditions too. A theorem using one remains conditional on that precise assumption; failure of the assumption alone neither proves nor disproves the theorem's conclusion.

title: Balance includes geometric comparison
body: Local energy-momentum balance must compare tensor quantities at neighbouring events. In curved spacetime the connection supplies that comparison. For the total matter source with its equations of motion satisfied, the conservation statement is \(\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\).

title: Expand the divergence
body:
The tensor derivative gives \[
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu T^{\mu
u}+\Gamma^\mu{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda
u}+\Gamma^
u{}_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}.\] The two connection terms act on different indices. They can be removed at one event in a local inertial chart, but not generally across a finite region. Even flat spacetime needs them in curvilinear coordinates.

title: Consistency of the coupled equations
body:
For constant \(\Lambda\), taking the divergence of Einstein's equation gives \[\kappa
abla^\mu T_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{EFE}}{=}
abla^\mu G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda
abla^\mu g_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{Bianchi, compatibility}}{=}0.\] The same matter conservation follows from diffeomorphism invariance of the matter action when the matter fields obey their equations. A subsystem exchanging energy with other fields need not be separately conserved.

title: A symmetry can supply a conserved charge
body:
If a vector field \(\xi\) generates an isometry, it obeys the Killing equation \(
abla_\mu\xi_
u+
abla_
u\xi_\mu=0\). Symmetry of stress-energy then makes \(J^\mu\coloneqq T^{\mu
u}\xi_
u\) divergence-free. Integrating this vector current gives a conserved charge when boundary flux vanishes. A timelike symmetry supplies an energy interpretation.

title: Local balance is not universal global energy
body: A generic spacetime has no time-translation symmetry. One cannot simply add coordinate energy components at different events and infer a conserved total from the tensor divergence. Boundary or asymptotic constructions can provide gravitational energy in appropriate settings, but require additional structure.

title: Supply material physics
body: Einstein's equations couple geometry to matter but do not specify how a material's pressure depends on its thermodynamic state. An equation of state supplies this constitutive information. Together with conservation and a fluid model, it closes the evolution problem.

title: A simple barotropic model
body: A barotropic fluid assumes \(p=p(\epsilon)\), where \(\epsilon\) is rest-frame energy density. A useful idealisation is the model law \[p=w\epsilon,\qquad w\coloneqq p/\epsilon\quad(\epsilon\ne0).\] The first equation assumes constant \(w\) when used as a linear equation of state; the ratio definition alone does not assert that constancy. Pressure and energy density have the same units.

title: Three distinct responses
body: Pressureless dust uses \(w=0\); isotropic radiation uses \(w=1/3\); an effective cosmological source uses \(w=-1\). The last is not an ordinary gas with a preferred fluid rest frame. These examples are material assumptions or idealisations, rather than alternatives to the gravitational field equation.

title: Count the missing relation
body: On a given metric, a perfect fluid has energy density, pressure and three independent velocity components. Its four conservation equations leave one constitutive relation to supply. More general materials need additional variables such as particle density, entropy or composition, with their own equations; a single barotropic relation is then insufficient.

title: Sound speed is a derivative
body: For adiabatic perturbations of a suitable ordinary fluid, \(c_s^2=c^2(\partial p/\partial\epsilon)_s\), where entropy per particle is held fixed. Thus a constant barotropic law gives \(c_s^2=wc^2\). Stability and causal propagation constrain the derivative, not just the ratio \(p/\epsilon\). Do not interpret the vacuum relation \(w=-1\) as the sound speed of an ordinary fluid.

title: Couple geometry and matter
body: Einstein's equations determine how the metric responds to matter and non-gravitational fields. The metric also controls matter motion, so this is a coupled system rather than a one-way force prescription.

title: The atlas field equation
body:
With signature \(+---\), the glossary's Riemann definition and explicit \(c\), define \(\kappa\coloneqq8\pi G/c^4\). The field equation is \[G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}.\] The minus sign before \(\Lambda\) belongs to this complete convention; positive \(\Lambda\) represents positive effective vacuum energy. Sources using the opposite signature often write a plus sign. Comparing signs requires comparing curvature definitions too.

title: Why this combination works
body: The \cref{Einstein tensor}{gr.einstein_tensor} and constant metric term have zero covariant divergence. Their source must therefore obey \cref{covariant conservation}{gr.covariant_conservation}. The coupling is fixed by recovering Newton's Poisson equation for weak, slowly varying fields and nonrelativistic matter. Pressure and radiation remain sources beyond that limit.

title: Equations need data and a matter model
body: There are ten symmetric component equations in four dimensions, linked by four differential identities and coordinate freedom. Their initial-value formulation contains constraints as well as evolution equations. Solving requires appropriate initial or boundary data, a coordinate choice and matter dynamics; conservation alone does not select a unique spacetime.

title: Vacuum is not the absence of gravitational physics
body: Where \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\), curvature can still encode tides and gravitational waves. Nonlinear metric terms describe gravitational self-interaction without inserting a universal local gravitational stress-energy tensor on the right. The \cref{trace-reversed form}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} is often easier for calculations but describes the same theory.

title: A uniform geometric term
body: The cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) permits curvature even without ordinary matter. It has dimensions of inverse length squared and multiplies the metric, introducing no preferred observer direction at an event.

title: Move it to an effective source
body:
In our convention \(G_{\mu
u}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}\). Equivalently, \[G_{\mu
u}=\kappa(T_{\mu
u}+T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu
u}),\qquad T^{(\Lambda)}_{\mu
u}\coloneqq rac{\Lambda}{\kappa}g_{\mu
u}.\] This is an algebraic reassignment, not additional matter counted twice. If vacuum energy is already included in \(T\), its contribution must not also be repeated in \(\Lambda\).

title: Read its density and pressure
body: Comparing with the perfect-fluid form gives \[\epsilon_\Lambda\overset{\text{observer projection}}{=}\frac{\Lambda c^4}{8\pi G},\qquad p_\Lambda=-\epsilon_\Lambda.\] The combination \(\epsilon_\Lambda+p_\Lambda\) vanishes, removing dependence on a fluid velocity. Positive \(\Lambda\) therefore gives the same positive vacuum density to every timelike observer.

title: Curved empty spacetime
body: In four-dimensional ordinary vacuum, tracing the field equation gives \(R=-4\Lambda\) and hence \(R_{\mu\nu}=-\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}\) in our convention. Positive \(\Lambda\) permits de Sitter geometry and contributes an outward acceleration \(\Lambda c^2r/3\) in the weak static spherical limit. The sign of the Ricci scalar alone must not be used to infer attraction.

title: The equation does not explain the value
body: A metric-proportional source can model vacuum energy, but classical GR does not determine its microscopic origin or numerical value. Cosmological observations and quantum vacuum-energy calculations are separate subjects. A spacetime-varying replacement needs extra dynamics or energy exchange to remain compatible with the Bianchi identity.

title: Measure matter's response to geometry
body: Changing the metric changes distances, volume and the contractions in a matter action. The coefficient of that variation defines the Hilbert stress-energy tensor. This construction makes its role as the gravitational source explicit.

title: Vary the inverse metric
body:
Use \(c\overset{	ext{units}}{=}1\), signature \(+---\), and hold the matter fields fixed during metric variation. Define \[T_{\mu
u}\coloneqq rac{2}{\sqrt{-g}} rac{\delta S_m}{\delta g^{\mu
u}},\qquad\delta S_m= rac12\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu
u}\delta g^{\mu
u}.\] The functional derivative includes integrations by parts where required. This plus sign pairs with the negative gravitational action in the glossary.

title: A minimally coupled scalar example
body:
Take \(S_m=\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal L_m\), where \(\mathcal L_m\coloneqq	frac12g^{\alpha eta}\partial_\alpha\phi\partial_ eta\phi-V(\phi)\). Varying both the contraction and the determinant gives \[T_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{metric variation}}{=}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_
u\phi-g_{\mu
u}\mathcal L_m.\] The first contribution comes from \(g^{\alpha eta}\); the second from \(\sqrt{-g}\). Omitting the volume variation gives the wrong source.

title: Check physical energy
body: In a local orthonormal frame the scalar example gives \[T_{\hat0\hat0}=\tfrac12(\partial_{\hat0}\phi)^2+\tfrac12\sum_i(\partial_{\hat i}\phi)^2+V(\phi).\] For a nonnegative potential the measured energy density is nonnegative. This is a useful sign check against the chosen action, although it does not establish every energy condition.

title: Changing the varied variable changes a sign
body:
Because \(\delta g^{\mu
u}=-g^{\mu\alpha}g^{
u eta}\delta g_{\alpha eta}\), varying the covariant metric instead gives \(\delta S_m=-	frac12\int\sqrt{-g}\,T^{\mu
u}\delta g_{\mu
u}\,d^4x\). Symmetry of the metric variation gives a symmetric tensor. Its covariant conservation additionally uses the matter equations, not merely this definition.

title: Solve algebraically for Ricci
body: Trace reversal rewrites Einstein's equations as a direct relation between Ricci curvature and a trace-adjusted source. It changes the algebraic packaging, not the theory, and is particularly useful in the Newtonian and vacuum limits.

title: Take the four-dimensional trace
body:
Define \(T\coloneqq g^{\mu
u}T_{\mu
u}\). Starting with the atlas equation and using \(g^{\mu
u}g_{\mu
u}=4\), \[R-2R-4\Lambda\overset{	ext{traced EFE}}{=}\kappa T,\qquad R=-\kappa T-4\Lambda.\] The factor four is dimensional, not a consequence of the signature.

title: Substitute the trace back
body:
Rearrange the original equation as \(R_{\mu
u}=\kappa T_{\mu
u}+	frac12Rg_{\mu
u}+\Lambda g_{\mu
u}\). Substituting the trace gives \[R_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{trace substitution}}{=}\kappa\left(T_{\mu
u}-	frac12Tg_{\mu
u}ight)-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\] The minus cosmological sign agrees with the glossary. The adjusted source need not share all physical interpretations of the original stress-energy tensor.

title: Pressure remains in the source
body: For a perfect fluid in its orthonormal rest frame, \(T=\epsilon-3p\). Therefore \[R_{\hat0\hat0}\overset{\text{perfect fluid}}{=}\frac{\kappa}{2}(\epsilon+3p)-\Lambda.\] This helps explain why relativistic pressure gravitates. It is a local curvature relation, not by itself an equation for a star's total mass.

title: The coefficient depends on dimension
body: In \(n>2\) dimensions the source trace coefficient is \(1/(n-2)\), and the cosmological term here is \(-2\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}/(n-2)\). The familiar one half is specific to four dimensions. In two dimensions this inversion fails because the Einstein tensor vanishes identically.

title: Remove matter locally, not curvature
body: An ordinary vacuum region has \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\). It can lie outside a star or black hole even though matter elsewhere helped determine its geometry. Vacuum is a local source condition, not a statement that nothing gravitational happens there.

title: Zero cosmological constant
body: In four dimensions with \(\Lambda=0\), the field equation gives \(G_{\mu\nu}=0\). Taking the trace yields \(R=0\), so \[R_{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{vacuum EFE}}{=}0.\] This is Ricci-flatness. It constrains a contraction of Riemann, leaving possible Weyl curvature and tidal effects.

title: Schwarzschild is curved vacuum
body: Outside a spherical body the Schwarzschild solution has zero Ricci tensor but \(K=48(GM/c^2)^2/r^6\). Thus a freely falling cloud can deform despite the absence of local matter. \cref{Gravitational waves}{gr.gravitational_waves} also illustrate vacuum curvature carrying physical tidal information.

title: Retaining the cosmological term
body:
With ordinary matter absent but \(\Lambda
e0\), the atlas trace-reversed equation instead gives \[R_{\mu
u}\overset{T_{\mu
u}=0}{=}-\Lambda g_{\mu
u}.\] This is not Ricci-flat. State whether vacuum includes an explicit cosmological term or whether that term has been absorbed into an effective stress-energy source.

title: Vacuum equations do not select Schwarzschild alone
body: A solution still needs symmetry assumptions and suitable data. Schwarzschild describes spherical vacuum with zero cosmological constant; rotating or time-dependent vacuum geometries need not share its form. Boundary conditions retain information about sources outside the region in which the vacuum equation is being solved.

title: Approximate a region by a flat background
body: Weak-field theory describes a metric close to Minkowski form across a useful region in suitable coordinates. This is stronger than local flatness at one event and does not require that all sources or test particles move slowly.

title: Choose a background split
body:
Define the perturbation by \(h_{\mu
u}\coloneqq g_{\mu
u}-\eta_{\mu
u}\), with \(|h_{\mu
u}|\ll1\) in the chosen background chart. To first order, \[g^{\mu
u}\simeq\eta^{\mu
u}-h^{\mu
u},\qquad h^{\mu
u}\coloneqq\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}h_{\alpha eta}.\] Multiplying this inverse by \(g_{\mu
u}\) cancels the linear correction; products of perturbations are discarded.

title: Connection and curvature at first order
body:
The Levi-Civita formula becomes \[\Gamma^ho{}_{\mu
u}\simeq	frac12\eta^{ho\sigma}(\partial_\mu h_{\sigma
u}+\partial_
u h_{\sigma\mu}-\partial_\sigma h_{\mu
u}).\] Curvature contains second derivatives of \(h\) at this order; the quadratic connection terms enter later. Small metric amplitude need not mean slow time variation, as weak gravitational waves illustrate.

title: A static Newtonian source
body: For slowly moving matter with negligible pressure and anisotropic stress, a convenient isotropic weak-field chart gives \[ds^2\simeq(1+2\Phi/c^2)c^2dt^2-(1-2\Phi/c^2)\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j.\] Here \(\Phi\) is the Newtonian potential and \(\Lambda\) is neglected. Both time and spatial components change; ignoring the latter loses part of the light-deflection result.

title: Gauge and approximation are different choices
body: A small coordinate change changes the components of \(h\), so their smallness is assessed in an appropriate chart, not every possible chart. Linearisation discards nonlinear terms after that choice. The \cref{Newtonian limit}{gr.newtonian_limit} adds slow motion and approximate stationarity; the \cref{post-Newtonian scheme}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} keeps selected nonlinear terms consistently.
